title: Working capital and term loan documentation checklist for brokers
summary: The documents lenders ask for on $100K–$750K working capital and term loans, how the list changes by lender type, the gaps that stall files, and a checklist.
body_markdown:
A broker sends a lender a $400,000 working capital request for a regional food distributor: the application, two years of tax returns and three months of bank statements. A week later the file comes back with a list. The lender wants a year-to-date balance sheet, a receivables aging, a schedule of existing debt, and an explanation for a fixed debit that leaves the operating account every business day and appears nowhere else in the file. The distributor is invented; the list will be familiar.


Every item on it was coming eventually, and each round of asks costs the deal time and the borrower’s patience. This guide puts the list up front.


Quick answer


For a small-business working capital or term loan, lenders typically ask for a signed application, recent business bank statements, two or three years of business and personal tax returns, a year-to-date P&L and balance sheet, receivable and payable agings, a schedule of existing debt, entity and ownership documents, ID for the owners and an itemized use of funds.


Non-bank lenders often start with less on smaller deals. Banks and SBA lenders usually want the full set. Either way, a file is lender-ready when it is complete, current and its documents agree with each other.


Key takeaways


-


Get the lender’s own list first. The same deal draws different asks from a non-bank lender, a bank and an SBA lender.


-


Lender-ready means complete, current and consistent. Underwriters read documents against each other, so a file can have everything and still stall.


-


The gaps that send files back are usually small: a missing page, a stale interim, a loan payment on the bank statement that is not on the debt schedule.


01


## The documents lenders ask for, and what each one answers


Working capital and term loans draw on the same core file. A working capital request puts more weight on receivables, payables and cash; a term loan puts more on what is being bought and whether the term fits it. Every lender adds or drops items.


The documents lenders typically ask for on a working capital or term loan Document What the lender reads it for What complete usually looks like


Application Who the business and its owners are, what is being asked for, and what the business already owes. The lender’s own form, signed. For SBA 7(a) loans, SBA Form 1919.\[2\]


Business bank statements Real deposits, balances, overdrafts and returned items, and any loan payments missing from the debt schedule. The most recent months, every page, for every operating account.\[1\]


Business tax returns The history the lender trusts most, because it can be checked against IRS transcripts. Usually two or three years, signed, with every schedule and statement.\[1,4\]


Personal tax returns Income and obligations of the owners who will guarantee the loan, and pass-through income for S corporations and partnerships. The same years as the business returns, for each guarantor.


Interim P&L and balance sheet Whether the business has held up since the last return. Year to date, dated, ideally with the same period a year earlier beside it.\[1\]


AR and AP agings Who owes the business, who it owes, and how late each balance is. By customer and by supplier, in aging buckets, as of the interim balance sheet date.\[5\]


Debt schedule Every payment the new loan has to sit beside, which feeds debt service coverage. Each creditor, original amount, balance, payment, rate, maturity, collateral and status, including shareholder loans.\[1\]


Personal financial statement What each guarantor owns and owes outside the business. One per guarantor, dated. For SBA loans, Form 413 or the lender’s equivalent.\[1,3\]


Entity documents That the borrower exists, is in good standing and that the signers can bind it. Formation documents, operating agreement or bylaws, good standing, EIN confirmation, any DBA.


Ownership and control Who must be identified and verified, and who will be asked to guarantee. Every owner and percentage, adding to 100%, including owners held through other entities.\[1,6\]


Owner identification Identity verification for owners, guarantors and signers. Current government-issued photo ID for each.\[6\]


Use of funds That the amount matches a real need, and the term matches what it buys. An itemized breakdown, with quotes or invoices for anything purchased.\[1\]


### Tax returns are checked against the IRS


Lenders lean on tax returns because they can be verified. Through the IRS Income Verification Express Service, a borrower signs Form 4506-C so a lender can receive transcripts, and the IRS only releases tax records to a third party with the taxpayer’s consent.\[4\] On an SBA 7(a) loan, the lender must obtain transcripts and reconcile any differences with the applicant’s financial data before the first disbursement.\[1\] A draft return, or an original that was later amended, will show up at that step, so send what was filed.


### The interim and the agings show the present


A tax return can be well over a year old by the time a deal is packaged. The year-to-date P&L and balance sheet tell the lender whether the business has held up since. On a 7(a) Small loan, SBA wants interim statements dated within 120 days of submission.\[1\]


An aging lists receivables or payables by customer or supplier and shows how current or late each balance is.\[5\] It answers the questions a balance sheet cannot: are the receivables collectible, and is the business stretching its suppliers to fund itself? Lenders normally treat receivables as concentrated when a single account is 10% or more of the total, and in receivables financing, accounts more than three times past terms, 90 days on 30-day terms, are usually treated as ineligible.\[5\]


### The debt schedule has to be complete


Debt service coverage compares cash flow with every payment the business makes, so a missing debt overstates it. SBA’s standard 7(a) procedures call a current debt schedule prepared by the applicant, including any shareholder debt, important to a complete analysis, and on a 7(a) Small loan the lender reviews the two most recent months of the primary operating account specifically to confirm that every debt is in the calculation.\[1\] That is the fixed daily debit from the opening: if it is on the bank statement, it belongs on the schedule.


### Owners, guarantors and use of funds


Banks must identify and verify each individual who owns 25% or more of a business customer, plus one individual with significant control.\[6\] SBA goes further: the lender records 100% of the applicant’s direct and indirect owners, any individual owning 20% or more must give an unlimited full guaranty, and each guarantor’s personal financial statement must be dated within 90 days of approval.\[1\] For SBA loans that statement is usually Form 413 or the lender’s equivalent.\[3\]


“Working capital” on its own is not a use of funds. On an SBA 7(a) loan where half or more of the proceeds will go to working capital, the lender has to explain in its credit memo why that much is necessary.\[1\] Give the lender the breakdown that lets them write that paragraph: inventory for a named contract, payroll through a seasonal gap, a supplier who wants shorter terms.


02


## How the list changes with deal size and lender type


Small businesses that apply for credit still go to large banks most often, but online lenders have taken a growing share: 29% of applicants sought financing at one in the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey, up from 17% in 2020.\[7\] The three channels a broker most often packages for ask for different things.


### Non-bank lenders


Online lenders use traditional measures such as credit scores alongside business data such as card sales, and many get direct online access to a borrower’s accounting software, merchant accounts and payroll data.\[8\] On smaller requests that can mean a short application, recent bank statements or an account connection, ID and entity documents. As the request grows, non-bank lenders typically move toward a bank-style file with tax returns, an interim and a debt schedule. Expect the debt schedule early here too: lenders in this channel typically check whether the business already carries other short-term financing.


### Banks


A bank’s conventional term loan or line usually wants the full file in the table, often with the prior-year period beside the interim, and its own forms for the application and personal financial statement. Borrowers notice: one bank applicant in a Federal Reserve focus group said the process “was very clear but time consuming,” because the bank needed “a lot of information for the application, which is not always easily accessible.”\[8\]


### SBA 7(a) lenders, and the $350,000 line


SBA’s rules make the deal-size shift explicit. A 7(a) Small loan, up to $350,000, lets the lender use the same credit analysis it uses for its similarly sized conventional loans, including credit scoring models its regulator permits. The lender reviews two months of operating account activity, and debt service coverage must be at least 1.10.\[1\]


Above $350,000 the loan is a Standard 7(a). The credit analysis for an existing business rests on the three most recent years of historical financial information plus an interim statement, with the debt schedule, a spread of the pro-forma balance sheet, ratio calculations and coverage of at least 1.15.\[1\] That spread is built from exactly the documents in this guide; our[guide to financial spreading](https://www.kita.ai/blog/what-is-financial-spreading) shows what the lender’s analyst does with them.\[9\]

A broad pattern for $100K to $750K working capital and term loans, not a rule: individual lenders differ, and the ask grows with the size of the request. The SBA column reflects SOP 50 10 8.1 where it sets a requirement; everything else describes typical practice. Get each lender's own list before you collect anything.


03


## What makes a file lender-ready


A lender-ready file is the one an underwriter can start on without writing back. That comes down to four things:


-


**Complete against this lender’s list.** Every item they asked for, every page of each, for every entity and owner it applies to.


-


**Current.** Interim statements, bank statements and personal financial statements dated recently enough that the lender will not ask for new ones before approval.


-


**Consistent.** The documents agree with each other, or the difference is explained. This is where most of the questions come from.


-


**Explained.** A one-page cover memo that states the request, itemizes the use of funds and answers the questions an underwriter will have before they ask them.


Consistency is the part lenders always check. When the analyst spreads the financials, every figure lands beside figures from other documents, and any disagreement becomes a question. Read these pairs against each other before you submit:


### Five places a file has to agree with itself


Underwriters read documents against each other. These are the pairs to check before you submit.


1. Bank statements


⟷


Debt schedule


Every recurring loan payment on the statements appears on the schedule.


2. Interim balance sheet


⟷


AR and AP agings


The agings total to the receivables and payables on the same date.


3. Tax returns


⟷


IRS transcripts


The returns in the file match what was filed.


4. Tax returns


⟷


Interim P&L


The interim follows on from the last return, or the difference is explained.


5. Ownership breakdown


⟷


Guarantor documents


Owners add to 100%, and everyone who must guarantee has a full set of documents.


A schematic of common cross-checks, not a complete list. A file can be complete and still stall if two of its documents disagree and nothing explains why.


04


## Common gaps that stall files


Files rarely stall on a big problem. They stall on small gaps that take rounds of back-and-forth to close:


-


**Partial bank statements.** A summary page instead of the full statement, one operating account of two, or a skipped month.


-


**Stale dates.** An interim that was current when you started the file but not when it was submitted, or a personal financial statement that will be more than 90 days old at an SBA approval.\[1\]


-


**Returns that are not the filed returns.** Unsigned copies, missing schedules, or an original that was later amended. Transcripts will show the difference.\[1,4\]


-


**A debt on the bank statement that is not on the schedule.** Daily or weekly debits from short-term financing, an equipment lease, a loan from an owner. It changes coverage and raises a question about what else is missing.\[1\]


-


**Agings that do not tie, or one customer carrying the book.** An aging that does not total to the balance sheet, old balances nobody has written off, or a single customer at 10% or more of receivables with no word about who they are.\[5\]


-


**Ownership that does not reach 100%.** A holding company with its own owners, a spouse with a stake, a partner who left on paper but not in the operating agreement. Each one can add a guarantor and a set of documents.\[1,6\]


-


**A vague use of funds.** A round number labelled “working capital” with no breakdown behind it.\[1\]


-


**Names that do not match.** The legal name on the application, a trade name on the bank statements and an old name on the returns, with nothing linking them.


-


**Refinancing without the paper.** If the loan pays off existing debt, have the notes and the recent payment history. SBA’s rules ask for the notes being refinanced and a written explanation of any late payments in the past 12 months.\[1\]


05


## Putting the package together, in six steps


Asking the borrower once, for the right things, is most of the work.


1. 01


Start from the lender’s own list


Every lender’s checklist differs, and an SBA lender, a bank and a non-bank lender will ask for different things on the same deal. Get the list for the product and size before you ask the borrower for anything, so you ask once.


2. 02


Collect complete documents, not convenient ones


Every page of every bank statement, for every operating account. Signed tax returns with all schedules. A balance sheet with the profit and loss, not instead of it. A missing page reads as something hidden.


3. 03


Make the numbers agree with each other


The interim should follow on from the tax returns. The agings should total to the receivables and payables on the interim balance sheet. Every loan payment on the bank statements should appear on the debt schedule.\[1,5\]


4. 04


Check the dates


Interim statements, bank statements and personal financial statements go stale. On a 7(a) Small loan, SBA wants interim statements dated within 120 days of submission, and on SBA loans the guarantors’ personal financial statements must be dated within 90 days of approval.\[1\]


5. 05


Account for every owner


List every owner and percentage until the total reaches 100%, including owners behind holding companies, and collect ID and personal documents from everyone the lender will need to identify or ask to guarantee.\[1,6\]


6. 06


Write the cover memo


One page: what the business does, what it is asking for and why, the itemized use of funds, and a plain explanation of anything an underwriter will question, such as a dip in revenue, a late payment or one customer carrying most of the receivables.\[1,5\]


06


## The checklist


A working list for a $100K to $750K working capital or term loan. Treat it as a starting point and line it up against each lender’s own requirements before you send it to the borrower.


The request


-


Completed, signed application (SBA Form 1919 for 7(a) loans)


-


Amount, product and term requested


-


Itemized use of funds, with quotes or invoices for purchases


-


One-page cover memo, including explanations for anything unusual


Business financials


-


Business tax returns, usually two or three years, signed, all schedules


-


Year-end financial statements, noting whether company-prepared, compiled, reviewed or audited


-


Year-to-date P&L and balance sheet, dated, with the prior-year period if available


-


Business bank statements: recent months, every page, every operating account


-


AR and AP agings dated the same day as the interim balance sheet


-


Debt schedule covering every business debt, including shareholder loans


-


Copies of the notes for any debt the loan will refinance


Owners and guarantors


-


Ownership breakdown that adds to 100%, including indirect owners


-


Personal tax returns for each guarantor, same years as the business


-


Personal financial statement for each guarantor, dated


-


Government-issued photo ID for each owner, guarantor and signer


-


Signed consents for credit reports and IRS transcripts (Form 4506-C or the lender’s equivalent)


The entity


-


Articles of incorporation or organization


-


Operating agreement, partnership agreement or bylaws


-


Certificate of good standing


-


EIN confirmation and any DBA filings


-


Business licenses the business needs to operate


If they apply


-


Collateral list with descriptions and estimated values


-


Business lease or mortgage statement


-


Franchise agreement


-


Explanation of any late payments in the last 12 months on debt being refinanced

## Frequently asked questions


### What documents are required for a business term loan?


Most lenders ask for a signed application, recent business bank statements, two or three years of business tax returns, personal tax returns for the guarantors, a year-to-date profit and loss and balance sheet, a schedule of existing business debt, entity and ownership documents, ID for the owners and an itemized use of funds. Larger requests and bank or SBA loans usually add receivable and payable agings, personal financial statements and authorization to pull IRS transcripts. The exact list varies by lender, so get theirs first.


### What documents do I need for a working capital loan?


The same core file as a term loan, with more attention on the short-term picture: recent bank statements, a current interim balance sheet, accounts receivable and accounts payable agings, and a debt schedule that shows every payment the business already makes. Lenders want to see why the business needs the cash and how the cycle of receivables, inventory and payables will repay it. For an SBA 7(a) loan where half or more of the proceeds go to working capital, the lender has to explain in its credit memo why that much is needed.


### How many months of bank statements do lenders want?


It varies. Many non-bank lenders lead with the most recent several months and may ask to connect to the account directly. For an SBA 7(a) Small loan, SBA requires the lender to review the two most recent months of activity on the primary operating account, to confirm every debt is in the coverage calculation. Whatever the number, send every page of every operating account for the months requested.


### What makes a loan package lender-ready?


A lender-ready package is complete against that lender’s list, current, and internally consistent: the interim follows on from the tax returns, the agings total to the balance sheet, every loan payment on the bank statements appears on the debt schedule, and the owners add up to 100%. It comes with a short cover memo that states the request and use of funds and explains anything an underwriter will question before they have to ask.


### Do non-bank lenders need tax returns and financial statements?


Often not on smaller deals, where many non-bank lenders work mainly from bank statements, credit and data pulled from the business’s accounts. As the request grows, non-bank lenders typically move toward a bank-style file with tax returns, an interim, a debt schedule and sometimes agings. If a deal could end up with a bank or SBA lender, it is worth collecting the full file early, so a change of lender does not mean a second round of asks.
